Chapter 4. Master and Slave Morality—Two Ways of Valuing
Picture this: it’s early morning, the world’s quiet, and your mind finally feels clear. In those peaceful moments, you might notice just how differently people value things. Some folks are drawn to strength, independence, and creativity, while others really cherish humility, obedience, and a sense of security.
Now, these aren’t just random preferences. They're the result of two very different ways of looking at the world.
Throughout history, every society has crafted its own system of values. In some, the highest virtues are strength, courage, and a bold sense of self. People who show these qualities? They get all the admiration, and their way of living becomes the gold standard. That’s what you might call the morality of the strong—of the masters—who set their own rules and create their own values.
On the flip side, there are societies where kindness, humility, and self-sacrifice top the list. Here, those who live with these qualities are praised, and their way of life becomes the model everyone looks up to. This is the morality of the weak—or the slaves—who follow rules handed down to them, finding meaning in obedience and acceptance.
Imagine a group of people who’ve always lived under someone else’s rule. They’re told that their suffering is noble, that being humble is a virtue, and that obedience will eventually pay off. Over time, they start to believe it. Their whole system of values grows out of this mindset—they see the strong as evil, and the weak as good.
But here’s something to pay attention to: this kind of morality isn’t some universal truth. It’s a response to their situation, a way to cope with feeling powerless and to make sense of their suffering. Meanwhile, the strong celebrate their own power and creativity—they see their values as a mark of their freedom.
Most people don’t realize just how much their own values are shaped by where they stand in society. The rules you follow, the virtues you look up to, the ideals you chase—they’re all rooted in a specific history and perspective.
So, the real challenge? It’s recognizing the limits of your own values—and finding the courage to create new ones. Only by moving beyond these old distinctions can we open the door to new, more creative and honest ways of living. Ways that truly affirm life, rather than just repeating the past.
